name: Treaty with the Appalachicola Band, 1833 (relinquishment by Econchatimico)
aka: Relinquishment by Econchatimico and his warriors of the Chattahoochee reserve, June 18, 1833
promises: Article 1: Econchatimico and his warriors gave up the reserve on the Chattahoochee made for them by the additional article of the Treaty of Camp Moultrie (1823).
Article 2: within three years, a patent to Econchatimico for himself, his sub-chiefs and warriors for three sections of land, laid off to take in their fields and improvements.

Article 3: their share of the $5,000 annuity under the Treaty of Camp Moultrie would continue while the Seminoles stayed in Florida, with the balance advanced when the Seminoles removed under the Treaty of Payne's Landing.
Article 4: if they gave up these grants and joined the Seminoles in the West under Payne's Landing, the United States would pay $3,000 for the reservation relinquished.
today: No court, Indian Claims Commission or government finding about this treaty was found. A local historian writes that Econchatimico was still on his former reserve in 1838, received the $3,000 in October 1838, and was then taken west under military escort.

openQuestions: Audit 2026-11-08: Kappler p. 398 prints two relinquishments of June 18, 1833. This file first described the one by Mulatto King and Tustenuggy Hajo (7 Stat. 427), which Royce schedules separately 'with the Appalachicola band' (area 184, treaties.json kappler-406). This record (area 185, 'certain chiefs in Florida') is Econchatimico's relinquishment of the Chattahoochee reserve, 7 Stat. 428; the file was rewritten for it.
Kappler gives no proclamation date for this second relinquishment; the first was proclaimed April 12, 1834. Not settled, so left out.

Whether the three-section patent was ever issued was not found; the historian's account suggests Econchatimico took the $3,000 under Article 4 instead. Federal land and removal records would settle it.
treaties.json lists the Seminole Tribe of Florida and the Miccosukee Tribe; the historian says descendants of the band live near Muskogee, Oklahoma. Not settled from a nation source.

2026-11-08 sweep: Court of Claims and ICC full text searched for Appalachicola, Apalachicola, Econchatimico and Chattahoochee 1833; only Seminole Docket 73 and Creek Docket 272 (an 1832 Alabama cession) came up; no Court of Claims case for the band. Nothing new.

plain.promised: Econchatimico's band gave up its Chattahoochee reserve for a patent to three sections of land within three years and its share of the annuity, or $3,000 if it moved west.
plain.happened: No court, claims commission or government finding about this treaty was found.
plain.today: Whether the patent was ever issued has not been traced; a historian says the chief took the $3,000 in 1838 and went west.
